hypotheses.statement: Among adults reporting no diagnosis, HbA1c>=6.5 is more prevalent in the not-insured than the insured group. Crude PR only, exploratory, no adjusted claim (L0017); association only.

Among adults with no reported diagnosis and HbA1c>=6.5, at least 60% have HbA1c in [6.5, 7.0). Cut-off 7.0 fixed, prediction 0.60 unchanged, exploratory (L0018); near-threshold share only, timing of onset is not testable.

question: Which discrepancy between self-reported diagnosis and HbA1c among US adults should we investigate next, and which subgroup merits confirmatory re-measurement? Cross-sectional, descriptive, no causal or clinical claims.

rivals.floor: 56.2% (CI 45.5-66.9, n=150, wt_mec) of no-diagnosis adults with HbA1c>=6.5 satisfy the tool-evaluated NGSP +/-5% band expression 'hba1c < 6.5 * 1.05' (calc_00014). Sensitivity only, not primary evidence (wt_fast, smaller fasting subsample): 39.4% of HbA1c>=6.5 have glucose<126 (calc_00013); 66.6% of glucose>=126 have HbA1c<6.5 (calc_00012). Cited assay reference: NGSP certification, 36 of 40 results within +/-5% of reference (https://ngsp.org/critsumm.asp).
rivals.statement: The HbA1c vs self-report/glucose discrepancy is largely assay and classification noise at the 6.5 threshold. Documented floor, not a hold-out test, no prediction (L0019). Floor (a) is the same cell fraction as the near-threshold share of H_recent_onset, so the two cannot be separated with this data (circularity stated). A single HbA1c per person cannot separate assay noise from true near-threshold values.

title: Undiagnosed diabetes: HbA1c vs self-report discrepancy (fast run)
